results.name: trial_index_yes_slope
results.description: Pearson correlation between trial_index and rating; the model has no time dependence (null ~0), so observed > null means people say "yes" more as the session goes on, observed < null means they grow more conservative.

results.name: near_target_distance_gradient
results.description: Yes-rate for targets within 5 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets 6-20 away; observed > null means people show a stronger numeric-similarity gradient than the model predicts, observed < null a weaker one.
results.code:
# name: near_target_distance_gradient
# description: Yes-rate for targets within 5 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets 6-20 away; observed > null means people show a stronger numeric-similarity gradient than the model predicts, observed < null a weaker one.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()[:, None]
    dmin = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    a = (dmin >= 1) & (dmin <= 5)
    b = (dmin >= 6) & (dmin <= 20)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: unanimity_rate
results.description: Fraction of (number_set, target) pairs whose repeated responses are all-yes or all-no; observed > null means people agree more (model posteriors too graded/intermediate), observed < null means people are noisier than the model's near-0/1 posteriors.

results.name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
results.description: Yes-rate for targets closer to the last-shown example than to the first minus yes-rate for targets closer to the first (multi-example sets); the model is order-invariant, so observed > null means a recency effect of example order, observed < null a primacy effect.
results.code:
# name: last_vs_first_example_proximity
# description: Yes-rate for targets closer to the last-shown example than to the first minus yes-rate for targets closer to the first (multi-example sets); the model is order-invariant, so observed > null means a recency effect of example order, observed < null a primacy effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    parts = df["number_set"].str.split(",")
    first = pd.to_numeric(parts.str[0]).to_numpy(float)
    last = pd.to_numeric(parts.str[-1]).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = df["number_set"].str.count(",").to_numpy() + 1
    dl = np.abs(t - last); dfst = np.abs(t - first)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    a = (n >= 2) & (dl < dfst); b = (n >= 2) & (dfst < dl)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: set_size_yes_contrast
results.description: Overall yes-rate for 4-example sets minus that for 1-2-example sets; observed > null means people tighten generalisation with more examples less than the model's size principle predicts, observed < null means they tighten more.

results.name: inside_hull_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets strictly between the smallest and largest example (not themselves examples); observed > null means people fill in the example range more than the model, observed < null means the model over-predicts interval-style "yes" inside the range.
results.code:
# name: inside_hull_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate for targets strictly between the smallest and largest example (not themselves examples); observed > null means people fill in the example range more than the model, observed < null means the model over-predicts interval-style "yes" inside the range.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.any(ex == t[:, None], axis=1)
    mask = (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~member
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy(float)[mask].mean())

results.name: far_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate for targets lying >= 25 away from every example; observed > null means people over-generalise to distant numbers (the model's rules/size principle under-produce far "yes"), observed < null means the model over-generalises far away.

results.name: parity_violation_yes_rate
results.description: Among sets whose examples all share one parity, the yes-rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed > null means people respect the shared-parity rule less than the model (model too rule-strict), observed < null means more.
results.code:
# name: parity_violation_yes_rate
# description: Among sets whose examples all share one parity, the yes-rate for targets of the opposite parity; observed > null means people respect the shared-parity rule less than the model (model too rule-strict), observed < null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(float)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.nan, ex % 2)
    pmax = np.nanmax(par, axis=1); pmin = np.nanmin(par, axis=1)
    same = pmax == pmin
    tpar = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy() % 2
    mask = same & (tpar != pmin)
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].to_numpy(float)[mask].mean())
